title: Salt in the water
hookLine: Uddalaka has his son drop salt in water overnight. by morning it's invisible, and still in every sip
carry: jnana is seeing what is, not choosing a belief

cards: Shvetaketu still doesn't get it. So his father, Uddalaka, tries something simple. Put this salt in water, he says, and come back in the morning.
Next day: bring me the salt. Shvetaketu looks. He can't find it; it has dissolved.
Take a sip from the top, his father says. How is it? Salty.
From the middle? Salty. From the bottom?

teach.b: Notice what happens: Shvetaketu doesn't decide the water is salty. The taste decides.
Shankara makes the same point on the Brahma Sutra's second line, which says Brahman is that from which this world is born, held and dissolved. Couldn't you just reason your way to a cause?
Not on its own, he says; the line gathers the Upanishads' teachings, and reasoning is welcome as their helper, because the senses can't show Brahman. Then his well-known contrast.

With action you have choices: do a ritual, skip it, do it another way. Knowing isn't like that. A tall shape glimpsed in poor light may be a post or a man; you can think either, but only one thought is knowledge.
Knowing depends on the thing, not on anyone's choosing.
Brahman is something that already is, so knowing it isn't picking a belief, and, he says, it's meant to end in direct experience, anubhava, like the taste of salt.

That's the Hindu path of jnana: not opinion, but seeing what is. Ramanuja and others join this knowing to loving meditation; Shankara draws his line firmly here. Today faith is often called a personal preference.
This tradition says the deepest truth isn't up for choosing; it waits to be tasted.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, study of the Upanishads with a teacher is followed by reflection and meditation, so that what is heard becomes direct understanding.

o: a duty you may choose to do or to skip
a feeling of peace that comes after prayer
knowing what is, settled by the thing itself

games.q: salt and fog — tap the pairs.
p: can be done, skipped, or done another way
only one thought about it is knowledge
meant to end in direct experience

s: Shvetaketu found the salt by looking hard
he couldn't see it at all. he knew it by tasting, from the top, the middle and the bottom.
Shankara says knowing depends on the thing, not on the knower's choice
post, man, or something else: only one thought about the post is knowledge.
for Shankara, knowing Brahman ends in words alone
he says it is meant to culminate in direct experience.

games.q: in the fog you see a tall shape. you'd rather it were a post, not a stranger. can you make it a post by deciding?
o: yes, if you decide firmly enough.
no, the thing itself settles it.
it's whatever most people say it is.
games.why: Shankara's point exactly: action depends on the doer, but knowledge depends on the thing.

practice: Take a sip of water, or simply notice your breath. Say silently the words Uddalaka spoke: you are that.

Don't argue with them or try to believe them hard; let them sit, the way salt sits in water, and come back to them whenever the mind wanders. Vedanta teachers call this manana, turning over what you've heard.
If you pray, let this quiet attention be your prayer; if you don't, simply rest in it.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing. For Shankara, knowing that depends on the thing itself, not on anyone's choosing, and that is meant to end in direct experience.

orig.note: Sanskrit: direct experience; Shankara says knowing Brahman is meant to culminate in it.

carryVoice: Your line: jnana is seeing what is, not choosing a belief. The salt was in every sip. Go gently.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 (salt dissolved in water: tasted from the top, the middle and the bottom; 'you do not see it, but it is here'; that is the real, that is the self, you are that)
Brahma Sutra 1.1.2 (that from which the origin and so on of this world come)

Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.2 (the sutra strings together Upanishad texts, with reasoning as an aid; action depends on the person, knowledge on the thing; the post that might be a man; knowledge of Brahman culminates in experience)
